subject: Agriculture
title: Wheat: The Global Staple
description: A short lesson to help you apply Wheat: The Global Staple.

hook.text: Wheat feeds more people than any other crop. It covers more farmland than any plant on Earth.

buildup.text: Domesticated 10,000 years ago from wild emmer, wheat's gluten makes bread possible—no other grain does this.

discovery.text: Modern bread wheat is a hexaploid—it has six sets of chromosomes from three ancestral grass species merged together.

twist.text: That genetic complexity makes wheat hard to improve. Its genome is five times larger than the human genome.

climax.text: The wheat genome was only fully sequenced in 2018—decades after rice and corn. Size was the obstacle.

punchline.text: The world's most important crop has the most complicated genetics.

quiz.question: Why is wheat's genome so difficult to work with?
options: It's hexaploid with six chromosome sets and five times larger than the human genome

details.summary: Wheat is the world's most widely grown cereal, feeding billions through bread, pasta, and flour products. This topic covers wheat's domestication, modern breeding advances, and the global trade networks that make wheat a geopolitical commodity.
details.whyItMatters: Wheat supplies about 20% of global dietary protein and calories. Disruptions to wheat supply—from war, drought, or disease—immediately affect food prices and hunger worldwide.
takeaways: Wheat is grown on more land area than any other food crop globally
Bread wheat is a polyploid species with three combined genomes from wild grasses
Russia, the EU, and the US are the top wheat exporters affecting global prices

faq.question: Why is wheat so important for global food security?
faq.answer: Wheat provides around 20% of the calories and protein consumed by humans worldwide. It is the primary staple grain for Europe, the Middle East, North Africa, and Central Asia, and is traded more extensively than any other food crop.

faq.question: What makes bread wheat genetically unique?
faq.answer: Bread wheat is a hexaploid—it contains six sets of chromosomes from three different wild grass ancestors that hybridized naturally over millennia. This large, complex genome gives wheat exceptional adaptability across diverse climates.
